crosswalk_notes: The 2019 course framework replaced the pre-2019 AP Calculus outline, in which content was listed as an unnumbered topic outline with no persistent identifiers. The current codes are three-part: a big idea prefix (CHA for Change, LIM for Limits, FUN for Analysis of Functions), an enduring understanding number, a learning objective letter, and an essential knowledge number, so FUN-6.D.2 reads as big idea Analysis of Functions, enduring understanding 6, learning objective D, essential knowledge statement 2. Because the enduring understanding numbers run independently within each big idea and the units draw learning objectives from several big ideas, code order does not follow unit order and a single learning objective can appear under several topics. No pre-2019 framework document is present in this project's cache, so the mapping between old outline entries and current codes is not established here [inferred].

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge CHA-1.A.1
essential_knowledge.text: Calculus uses limits to understand and model dynamic change.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge CHA-1.A.2
essential_knowledge.text: Because an average rate of change divides the change in one variable by the change in another, the average rate of change is undefined at a point where the change in the independent variable would be zero.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge CHA-1.A.3
essential_knowledge.text: The limit concept allows us to define instantaneous rate of change in terms of average rates of change.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge CHA-2.A.1
essential_knowledge.text: The difference quotients (f(a + h) - f(a))/h and (f(x) - f(a))/(x - a) express the average rate of change of a function over an interval.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge CHA-2.B.1
essential_knowledge.text: The instantaneous rate of change of a function at x = a can be expressed by lim as h approaches 0 of (f(a + h) - f(a))/h or lim as x approaches a of (f(x) - f(a))/(x - a), provided the limit exists. These are equivalent forms of the definition of the derivative and are denoted f'(a).

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge CHA-2.B.2
essential_knowledge.text: The derivative of f is the function whose value at x is lim as h approaches 0 of (f(x + h) - f(x))/h, provided this limit exists.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge CHA-2.B.3
essential_knowledge.text: For y = f(x), notations for the derivative include dy/dx, f'(x), and y'.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge CHA-2.B.4
essential_knowledge.text: The derivative can be represented graphically, numerically, analytically, and verbally.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge CHA-2.C.1
essential_knowledge.text: The derivative of a function at a point is the slope of the line tangent to a graph of the function at that point.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge CHA-2.D.1
essential_knowledge.text: The derivative at a point can be estimated from information given in tables or graphs.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge CHA-2.D.2
essential_knowledge.text: Technology can be used to calculate or estimate the value of a derivative of a function at a point.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge CHA-3.A.1
essential_knowledge.text: The derivative of a function can be interpreted as the instantaneous rate of change with respect to its independent variable.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge CHA-3.A.2
essential_knowledge.text: The derivative can be used to express information about rates of change in applied contexts.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge CHA-3.A.3
essential_knowledge.text: The unit for f'(x) is the unit for f divided by the unit for x.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge CHA-3.B.1
essential_knowledge.text: The derivative can be used to solve rectilinear motion problems involving position, speed, velocity, and acceleration.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge CHA-3.C.1
essential_knowledge.text: The derivative can be used to solve problems involving rates of change in applied contexts.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge CHA-3.D.1
essential_knowledge.text: The chain rule is the basis for differentiating variables in a related rates problem with respect to the same independent variable.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge CHA-3.D.2
essential_knowledge.text: Other differentiation rules, such as the product rule and the quotient rule, may also be necessary to differentiate all variables with respect to the same independent variable.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge CHA-3.E.1
essential_knowledge.text: The derivative can be used to solve related rates problems; that is, finding a rate at which one quantity is changing by relating it to other quantities whose rates of change are known.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge CHA-3.F.1
essential_knowledge.text: The tangent line is the graph of a locally linear approximation of the function near the point of tangency.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge CHA-3.F.2
essential_knowledge.text: For a tangent line approximation, the function’s behavior near the point of tangency may determine whether a tangent line value is an underestimate or an overestimate of the corresponding function value.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge CHA-3.G.1
essential_knowledge.text: Methods for calculating derivatives of real- valued functions can be extended to parametric functions.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge CHA-3.G.2
essential_knowledge.text: For a curve defined parametrically, the value of dy/dx at a point on the curve is the slope of the line tangent to the curve at that point. dy/dx, the slope of the line tangent to a curve defined using parametric equations, can be determined by dividing dy/dt by dx/dt, provided dx/dt does not equal zero.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge CHA-3.G.3
essential_knowledge.text: d^2y/dx^2 can be calculated by dividing d/dt of (dy/dx) by dx/dt.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge CHA-3.H.1
essential_knowledge.text: Methods for calculating derivatives of real- valued functions can be extended to vector- valued functions.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge CHA-4.A.1
essential_knowledge.text: The area of the region between the graph of a rate of change function and the x axis gives the accumulation of change.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge CHA-4.A.2
essential_knowledge.text: In some cases, accumulation of change can be evaluated by using geometry.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge CHA-4.A.3
essential_knowledge.text: If a rate of change is positive (negative) over an interval, then the accumulated change is positive (negative).

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge CHA-4.A.4
essential_knowledge.text: The unit for the area of a region defined by rate of change is the unit for the rate of change multiplied by the unit for the independent variable.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge CHA-4.B.1
essential_knowledge.text: The average value of a continuous function f over an interval [a, b] is 1/(b - a) times the integral from a to b of f(x) dx.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge CHA-4.C.1
essential_knowledge.text: For a particle in rectilinear motion over an interval of time, the definite integral of velocity represents the particle’s displacement over the interval of time, and the definite integral of speed represents the particle’s total distance traveled over the interval of time.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge CHA-4.D.1
essential_knowledge.text: A function defined as an integral represents an accumulation of a rate of change.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge CHA-4.D.2
essential_knowledge.text: The definite integral of the rate of change of a quantity over an interval gives the net change of that quantity over that interval.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge CHA-4.E.1
essential_knowledge.text: The definite integral can be used to express information about accumulation and net change in many applied contexts.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge CHA-5.A.1
essential_knowledge.text: Areas of regions in the plane can be calculated with definite integrals.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge CHA-5.A.2
essential_knowledge.text: Areas of regions in the plane can be calculated using functions of either x or y.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge CHA-5.A.3
essential_knowledge.text: Areas of certain regions in the plane may be calculated using a sum of two or more definite integrals or by evaluating a definite integral of the absolute value of the difference of two functions.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge CHA-5.B.1
essential_knowledge.text: Volumes of solids with square and rectangular cross sections can be found using definite integrals and the area formulas for these shapes.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge CHA-5.B.2
essential_knowledge.text: Volumes of solids with triangular cross sections can be found using definite integrals and the area formulas for these shapes.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge CHA-5.B.3
essential_knowledge.text: Volumes of solids with semicircular and other geometrically defined cross sections can be found using definite integrals and the area formulas for these shapes.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge CHA-5.C.1
essential_knowledge.text: Volumes of solids of revolution around the x- or y-axis may be found by using definite integrals with the disc method.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge CHA-5.C.2
essential_knowledge.text: Volumes of solids of revolution around any horizontal or vertical line in the plane may be found by using definite integrals with the disc method.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge CHA-5.C.3
essential_knowledge.text: Volumes of solids of revolution around the x- or y-axis whose cross sections are ring shaped may be found using definite integrals with the washer method.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge CHA-5.C.4
essential_knowledge.text: Volumes of solids of revolution around any horizontal or vertical line whose cross sections are ring shaped may be found using definite integrals with the washer method.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge CHA-5.D.1
essential_knowledge.text: The concept of calculating areas in rectangular coordinates can be extended to polar coordinates.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge CHA-5.D.2
essential_knowledge.text: Areas of regions bounded by polar curves can be calculated with definite integrals.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge CHA-6.A.1
essential_knowledge.text: The length of a planar curve defined by a function can be calculated using a definite integral.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge CHA-6.B.1
essential_knowledge.text: The length of a parametrically defined curve can be calculated using a definite integral.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-1.A.1
essential_knowledge.text: If f is a continuous function on the closed interval [a, b] and d is a number between f(a) and f(b), then the Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees that there is at least one number c between a and b, such that f(c) = d.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-1.B.1
essential_knowledge.text: If a function f is continuous over the interval [a, b] and differentiable over the interval (a, b), then the Mean Value Theorem guarantees a point within that open interval where the instantaneous rate of change equals the average rate of change over the interval.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-1.C.1
essential_knowledge.notes: Listed in the Fall 2026 clarifications as updated. The cached CED text already carries the updated wording, so the pre-2026 wording is not recoverable from this project's cache and previous_text is omitted [uncertain].
essential_knowledge.text: If a function f is continuous over the interval [a, b], then the Extreme Value Theorem guarantees that f has at least one minimum value and at least one maximum value on [a, b].

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-1.C.2
essential_knowledge.text: A point on a function where the first derivative equals zero or fails to exist is a critical point of the function.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-1.C.3
essential_knowledge.text: All local (relative) extrema occur at critical points of a function, though not all critical points are local extrema.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-2.A.1
essential_knowledge.text: If a function is differentiable at a point, then it is continuous at that point. In particular, if a point is not in the domain of f, then it is not in the domain of f '.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-2.A.2
essential_knowledge.text: A continuous function may fail to be differentiable at a point in its domain.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-3.A.1
essential_knowledge.text: Direct application of the definition of the derivative and specific rules can be used to calculate the derivative for functions of the form f(x) = x^r.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-3.A.2
essential_knowledge.text: Sums, differences, and constant multiples of functions can be differentiated using derivative rules.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-3.A.3
essential_knowledge.text: The power rule combined with sum, difference, and constant multiple properties can be used to find the derivatives for polynomial functions.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-3.A.4
essential_knowledge.text: Specific rules can be used to find the derivatives for sine, cosine, exponential, and logarithmic functions.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-3.B.1
essential_knowledge.text: Derivatives of products of differentiable functions can be found using the product rule.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-3.B.2
essential_knowledge.text: Derivatives of quotients of differentiable functions can be found using the quotient rule.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-3.B.3
essential_knowledge.text: Rearranging tangent, cotangent, secant, and cosecant functions using identities allows differentiation using derivative rules.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-3.C.1
essential_knowledge.text: The chain rule provides a way to differentiate composite functions.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-3.D.1
essential_knowledge.text: The chain rule is the basis for implicit differentiation.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-3.E.1
essential_knowledge.text: The chain rule and definition of an inverse function can be used to find the derivative of an inverse function, provided the derivative exists.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-3.E.2
essential_knowledge.text: The chain rule applied with the definition of an inverse function, or the formula for the derivative of an inverse function, can be used to find the derivatives of inverse trigonometric functions.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-3.F.1
essential_knowledge.text: Differentiating f' produces the second derivative f'', provided the derivative of f' exists; repeating this process produces higher-order derivatives of f.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-3.F.2
essential_knowledge.text: Higher-order derivatives are represented with a variety of notations. For y = f(x), notations for the second derivative include d^2y/dx^2, f''(x), and y''. Higher-order derivatives can be denoted d^n y/dx^n or f^(n)(x).

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-3.G.1
essential_knowledge.text: Methods for calculating derivatives of real- valued functions can be extended to functions in polar coordinates.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-3.G.2
essential_knowledge.text: For a curve given by a polar equation r = f(theta), derivatives of r, x, and y with respect to theta, and first and second derivatives of y with respect to x can provide information about the curve.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-4.A.1
essential_knowledge.text: The first derivative of a function can provide information about the function and its graph, including intervals where the function is increasing or decreasing.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-4.A.10
essential_knowledge.text: Graphical, numerical, and analytical information from f' and f'' can be used to predict and explain the behavior of f.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-4.A.11
essential_knowledge.text: Key features of the graphs of f, f', and f'' are related to one another.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-4.A.2
essential_knowledge.text: The first derivative of a function can determine the location of relative (local) extrema of the function.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-4.A.3
essential_knowledge.text: Absolute (global) extrema of a function on a closed interval can only occur at critical points or at endpoints.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-4.A.4
essential_knowledge.text: The graph of a function is concave up (down) on an open interval if the function’s derivative is increasing (decreasing) on that interval.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-4.A.5
essential_knowledge.text: The second derivative of a function provides information about the function and its graph, including intervals of upward or downward concavity.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-4.A.6
essential_knowledge.text: The second derivative of a function may be used to locate points of inflection for the graph of the original function.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-4.A.7
essential_knowledge.text: The second derivative of a function may determine whether a critical point is the location of a relative (local) maximum or minimum.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-4.A.8
essential_knowledge.text: When a continuous function has only one critical point on an interval on its domain and the critical point corresponds to a relative (local) extremum of the function on the interval, then that critical point also corresponds to the absolute (global) extremum of the function on the interval.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-4.A.9
essential_knowledge.text: Key features of functions and their derivatives can be identified and related to their graphical, numerical, and analytical representations.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-4.B.1
essential_knowledge.text: The derivative can be used to solve optimization problems; that is, finding a minimum or maximum value of a function on a given interval.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-4.C.1
essential_knowledge.text: Minimum and maximum values of a function take on specific meanings in applied contexts.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-4.D.1
essential_knowledge.text: A point on an implicit relation where the first derivative equals zero or does not exist is a critical point of the function.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-4.E.1
essential_knowledge.text: Applications of derivatives can be extended to implicitly defined functions.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-4.E.2
essential_knowledge.text: Second derivatives involving implicit differentiation may be relations of x, y, and dy/dx.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-5.A.1
essential_knowledge.text: The definite integral can be used to define new functions.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-5.A.2
essential_knowledge.text: If f is a continuous function on an interval containing a, then d/dx of (the integral from a to x of f(t) dt) = f(x), where x is in the interval.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-5.A.3
essential_knowledge.text: Graphical, numerical, analytical, and verbal representations of a function f provide information about the function g defined as g(x) = the integral from a to x of f(t) dt.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-6.A.1
essential_knowledge.text: In some cases, a definite integral can be evaluated by using geometry and the connection between the definite integral and area.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-6.A.2
essential_knowledge.text: Properties of definite integrals include the integral of a constant times a function, the integral of the sum of two functions, reversal of limits of integration, and the integral of a function over adjacent intervals.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-6.A.3
essential_knowledge.text: The definition of the definite integral may be extended to functions with removable or jump discontinuities.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-6.B.1
essential_knowledge.text: An antiderivative of a function f is a function g whose derivative is f.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-6.B.2
essential_knowledge.text: If a function f is continuous on an interval containing a, the function defined by F(x) = the integral from a to x of f(t) dt is an antiderivative of f for x in the interval.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-6.B.3
essential_knowledge.text: If f is continuous on the interval [a, b] and F is an antiderivative of f, then the integral from a to b of f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a).

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-6.C.1
essential_knowledge.text: The integral of f(x) dx is an indefinite integral of the function f and can be expressed as the integral of f(x) dx = F(x) + C, where F'(x) = f(x) and C is any constant.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-6.C.2
essential_knowledge.text: Differentiation rules provide the foundation for finding antiderivatives.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-6.C.3
essential_knowledge.text: Many functions do not have closed-form antiderivatives.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-6.D.1
essential_knowledge.text: Substitution of variables is a technique for finding antiderivatives.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-6.D.2
essential_knowledge.text: For a definite integral, substitution of variables requires corresponding changes to the limits of integration.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-6.D.3
essential_knowledge.text: Techniques for finding antiderivatives include rearrangements into equivalent forms, such as long division and completing the square.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-6.E.1
essential_knowledge.text: Integration by parts is a technique for finding antiderivatives.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-6.F.1
essential_knowledge.text: Some rational functions can be decomposed into sums of ratios of linear, nonrepeating factors to which basic integration techniques can be applied.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-7.A.1
essential_knowledge.text: Differential equations relate a function of an independent variable and the function’s derivatives.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-7.B.1
essential_knowledge.text: Derivatives can be used to verify that a function is a solution to a given differential equation.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-7.B.2
essential_knowledge.notes: Listed in the Fall 2026 clarifications as updated. The cached CED text already carries the updated wording, so the pre-2026 wording is not recoverable from this project's cache and previous_text is omitted [uncertain].
essential_knowledge.text: There may be infinitely many solutions to a differential equation.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-7.C.1
essential_knowledge.text: A slope field is a graphical representation of a differential equation on a finite set of points in the plane.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-7.C.2
essential_knowledge.text: Slope fields provide information about the behavior of solutions to first-order differential equations.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-7.C.3
essential_knowledge.text: Solutions to differential equations are functions or families of functions.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-7.C.4
essential_knowledge.text: Euler’s method provides a procedure for approximating a solution to a differential equation or a point on a solution curve.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-7.D.1
essential_knowledge.text: Some differential equations can be solved by separation of variables.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-7.D.2
essential_knowledge.text: Antidifferentiation can be used to find general solutions to differential equations.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-7.E.1
essential_knowledge.text: A general solution may describe infinitely many solutions to a differential equation. There is only one particular solution passing through a given point.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-7.E.2
essential_knowledge.text: The function F defined by F(x) = y sub 0 + the integral from a to x of f(t) dt is a particular solution to the differential equation dy/dx = f(x), satisfying F(a) = y sub 0.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-7.E.3
essential_knowledge.text: Solutions to differential equations may be subject to domain restrictions.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-7.F.1
essential_knowledge.text: Specific applications of finding general and particular solutions to differential equations include motion along a line and exponential growth and decay.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-7.F.2
essential_knowledge.text: The model for exponential growth and decay that arises from the statement “The rate of change of a quantity is proportional to the size of the quantity” is dy/dt = ky.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-7.G.1
essential_knowledge.text: The exponential growth and decay model, dy/dt = ky, with initial condition y = y sub 0 when t = 0, has solutions of the form y = y sub 0 e^(kt).

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-7.H.1
essential_knowledge.text: The model for logistic growth that arises from the statement “The rate of change of a quantity is jointly proportional to the size of the quantity and the difference between the quantity and the carrying capacity” is dy/dt = ky(a - y).

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-7.H.2
essential_knowledge.text: The logistic differential equation and initial conditions can be interpreted without solving the differential equation.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-7.H.3
essential_knowledge.text: The limiting value (carrying capacity) of a logistic differential equation as the independent variable approaches infinity can be determined using the logistic growth model and initial conditions.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-7.H.4
essential_knowledge.text: The value of the dependent variable in a logistic differential equation at the point when it is changing fastest can be determined using the logistic growth model and initial conditions.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-8.A.1
essential_knowledge.text: Methods for calculating integrals of real-valued functions can be extended to parametric or vector-valued functions.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-8.B.1
essential_knowledge.text: Derivatives can be used to determine velocity, speed, and acceleration for a particle moving along a curve in the plane defined using parametric or vector-valued functions.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge FUN-8.B.2
essential_knowledge.text: For a particle in planar motion over an interval of time, the definite integral of the velocity vector represents the particle’s displacement (net change in position) over the interval of time, from which we might determine its position. The definite integral of speed represents the particle’s total distance traveled over the interval of time.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-1.A.1
essential_knowledge.text: Given a function f, the limit of f(x) as x approaches c is a real number R if f(x) can be made arbitrarily close to R by taking x sufficiently close to c (but not equal to c). If the limit exists and is a real number, then the common notation is lim as x approaches c of f(x) = R.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-1.B.1
essential_knowledge.text: A limit can be expressed in multiple ways, including graphically, numerically, and analytically.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-1.C.1
essential_knowledge.text: The concept of a limit includes one sided limits.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-1.C.2
essential_knowledge.text: Graphical information about a function can be used to estimate limits.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-1.C.3
essential_knowledge.text: Because of issues of scale, graphical representations of functions may miss important function behavior.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-1.C.4
essential_knowledge.text: A limit might not exist for some functions at particular values of x. Some ways that the limit might not exist are if the function is unbounded, if the function is oscillating near this value, or if the limit from the left does not equal the limit from the right.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-1.C.5
essential_knowledge.text: Numerical information can be used to estimate limits.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-1.D.1
essential_knowledge.text: One-sided limits can be determined analytically or graphically.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-1.D.2
essential_knowledge.text: Limits of sums, differences, products, quotients, and composite functions can be found using limit theorems.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-1.E.1
essential_knowledge.text: It may be necessary or helpful to rearrange expressions into equivalent forms before evaluating limits.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-1.E.2
essential_knowledge.text: The limit of a function may be found by using the squeeze theorem.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-2.A.1
essential_knowledge.text: Types of discontinuities include removable discontinuities, jump discontinuities, and discontinuities due to vertical asymptotes.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-2.A.2
essential_knowledge.text: A function f is continuous at x = c provided that f(c) exists, lim as x approaches c of f(x) exists, and lim as x approaches c of f(x) = f(c).

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-2.B.1
essential_knowledge.text: A function is continuous on an interval if the function is continuous at each point in the interval.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-2.B.2
essential_knowledge.text: Polynomial, rational, power, exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric functions are continuous on all points in their domains.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-2.C.1
essential_knowledge.text: If the limit of a function exists at a discontinuity in its graph, then it is possible to remove the discontinuity by defining or redefining the value of the function at that point, so it equals the value of the limit of the function as x approaches that point.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-2.C.2
essential_knowledge.text: In order for a piecewise-defined function to be continuous at a boundary to the partition of its domain, the value of the expression defining the function on one side of the boundary must equal the value of the expression defining the other side of the boundary, as well as the value of the function at the boundary.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-2.D.1
essential_knowledge.text: The concept of a limit can be extended to include infinite limits.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-2.D.2
essential_knowledge.text: Asymptotic and unbounded behavior of functions can be described and explained using limits.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-2.D.3
essential_knowledge.text: The concept of a limit can be extended to include limits at infinity.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-2.D.4
essential_knowledge.text: Limits at infinity describe end behavior.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-2.D.5
essential_knowledge.text: Relative magnitudes of functions and their rates of change can be compared using limits.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-3.A.1
essential_knowledge.text: In some cases, recognizing an expression for the definition of the derivative of a function whose derivative is known offers a strategy for determining a limit.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-4.A.1
essential_knowledge.text: When the ratio of two functions tends to 0/0 or infinity/infinity in the limit, such forms are said to be indeterminate.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-4.A.2
essential_knowledge.text: Limits of the indeterminate forms 0/0 or infinity/infinity may be evaluated using L’Hospital’s Rule.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-5.A.1
essential_knowledge.text: Definite integrals can be approximated for functions that are represented graphically, numerically, analytically, and verbally.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-5.A.2
essential_knowledge.text: Definite integrals can be approximated using a left Riemann sum, a right Riemann sum, a midpoint Riemann sum, or a trapezoidal sum; approximations can be computed using either uniform or nonuniform partitions.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-5.A.3
essential_knowledge.text: Definite integrals can be approximated using numerical methods, with or without technology.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-5.A.4
essential_knowledge.text: Depending on the behavior of a function, it may be possible to determine whether an approximation for a definite integral is an underestimate or overestimate for the value of the definite integral.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-5.B.1
essential_knowledge.text: The limit of an approximating Riemann sum can be interpreted as a definite integral.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-5.B.2
essential_knowledge.text: A Riemann sum, which requires a partition of an interval I, is the sum of products, each of which is the value of the function at a point in a subinterval multiplied by the length of that subinterval of the partition.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-5.C.1
essential_knowledge.text: The definite integral of a continuous function f over the interval [a, b], denoted by the integral from a to b of f(x) dx, is the limit of Riemann sums as the widths of the subintervals approach 0. That is, the integral from a to b of f(x) dx = lim as the maximum of delta x sub i approaches 0 of the sum from i = 1 to n of f(x sub i star) delta x sub i, where n is the number of subintervals, delta x sub i is the width of the ith subinterval, and x sub i star is a value in the ith subinterval.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-5.C.2
essential_knowledge.text: A definite integral can be translated into the limit of a related Riemann sum, and the limit of a Riemann sum can be written as a definite integral.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-6.A.1
essential_knowledge.text: An improper integral is an integral that has one or both limits infinite or has an integrand that is unbounded in the interval of integration.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-6.A.2
essential_knowledge.text: Improper integrals can be determined using limits of definite integrals.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-7.A.1
essential_knowledge.text: The nth partial sum is defined as the sum of the first n terms of a series.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-7.A.10
essential_knowledge.text: The alternating series test is a method to determine whether an alternating series converges.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-7.A.11
essential_knowledge.text: The ratio test is a method to determine whether a series of numbers converges or diverges. X  EXCLUSION STATEMENT The nth term test for divergence, and the integral test, comparison test, limit comparison test, alternating series test, and ratio test for convergence are assessed on the AP Calculus BC Exam. Other methods are not assessed on the exam. However, teachers may include additional methods in the course, if time permits.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-7.A.12
essential_knowledge.text: A series may be absolutely convergent, conditionally convergent, or divergent.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-7.A.13
essential_knowledge.text: If a series converges absolutely, then it converges.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-7.A.14
essential_knowledge.text: If a series converges absolutely, then any series obtained from it by regrouping or rearranging the terms has the same value.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-7.A.2
essential_knowledge.text: An infinite series of numbers converges to a real number S (or has sum S), if and only if the limit of its sequence of partial sums exists and equals S.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-7.A.3
essential_knowledge.text: A geometric series is a series with a constant ratio between successive terms. bc only

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-7.A.4
essential_knowledge.text: If a is a real number and r is a real number such that |r| < 1, then the geometric series the sum from n = 0 to infinity of a r^n = a/(1 - r).

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-7.A.5
essential_knowledge.text: The nth term test is a test for divergence of a series.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-7.A.6
essential_knowledge.text: The integral test is a method to determine whether a series converges or diverges.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-7.A.7
essential_knowledge.text: In addition to geometric series, common series of numbers include the harmonic series, the alternating harmonic series, and p-series.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-7.A.8
essential_knowledge.text: The comparison test is a method to determine whether a series converges or diverges. bc only

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-7.A.9
essential_knowledge.text: The limit comparison test is a method to determine whether a series converges or diverges.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-7.B.1
essential_knowledge.text: If an alternating series converges by the alternating series test, then the alternating series error bound can be used to bound how far a partial sum is from the value of the infinite series.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-8.A.1
essential_knowledge.text: The coefficient of the nth degree term in a Taylor polynomial for a function f centered at x = a is f^(n)(a)/n!.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-8.A.2
essential_knowledge.text: In many cases, as the degree of a Taylor polynomial increases, the nth degree polynomial will approach the original function over some interval.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-8.B.1
essential_knowledge.text: Taylor polynomials for a function f centered at x = a can be used to approximate function values of f near x = a.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-8.C.1
essential_knowledge.text: The Lagrange error bound can be used to determine a maximum interval for the error of a Taylor polynomial approximation to a function.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-8.C.2
essential_knowledge.text: In some situations, the alternating series error bound can be used to bound the error of a Taylor polynomial approximation to the value of a function.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-8.D.1
essential_knowledge.text: A power series is a series of the form the sum from n = 0 to infinity of a sub n (x - r)^n, where n is a non-negative integer, {a sub n} is a sequence of real numbers, and r is a real number.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-8.D.2
essential_knowledge.text: If a power series converges, it either converges at a single point or has an interval of convergence.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-8.D.3
essential_knowledge.text: The ratio test can be used to determine the radius of convergence of a power series.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-8.D.4
essential_knowledge.text: The radius of convergence of a power series can be used to identify an open interval on which the series converges, but it is necessary to test both endpoints of the interval to determine the interval of convergence.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-8.D.5
essential_knowledge.text: If a power series has a positive radius of convergence, then the power series is the Taylor series of the function to which it converges over the open interval.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-8.D.6
essential_knowledge.text: The radius of convergence of a power series obtained by term-by-term differentiation or term- by-term integration is the same as the radius of convergence of the original power series.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-8.E.1
essential_knowledge.text: A Taylor polynomial for f (x) is a partial sum of the Taylor series for f (x).

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-8.F.1
essential_knowledge.text: The Maclaurin series for 1/(1 - x) is a geometric series.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-8.F.2
essential_knowledge.text: The Maclaurin series for sin x, cos x, and ex provides the foundation for constructing the Maclaurin series for other functions.

essential_knowledge.name: Essential knowledge LIM-8.G.1
essential_knowledge.text: Using a known series, a power series for a given function can be derived using operations such as term-by-term differentiation or term-by- term integration, and by various methods (e.g., algebraic processes, substitutions, or using properties of geometric series).
